newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: Azerbaijan to launch inter-bank currency market.
newsitem.headline: Azerbaijan to launch inter-bank currency market.

text.p: Azerbaijan plans to launch an inter-bank currency market to help pave the way for the full convertibility of the Azeri manat once the republic's new oil wealth starts reaching European markets, bankers said.

The ex-Soviet republic is beginning to benefit from reforms and multi-billion-dollar oil projects, and is moving fast to liberalise its economy. On Tuesday, trade officials in Geneva said Baku had applied to join the World Trade Organisation.
"Once their oil starts hitting European markets that will make convertibility much easier," one banker in the Azeri capital said.

The new market will next week for the first time allow banks to trade currency among themselves after daily auctions held at the Baku Interbank Currency Exchange (BICEX), said Samir Sharifov, head of foreign exchange dealing at the National Bank.

The bank, acting on the advice of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), will set a reference point for the Azeri currency in the new market and allow fluctuations within a narrow corridor, Sharifov told Reuters.
The range will probably be 0.5 percent on either side of the central point, he said.

Under the existing system, an Azeri bank is not allowed to sell foreign currency directly to corporate customers but must offer it through short morning auctions at BICEX where it will then bid on behalf of its clients.

Foreign banks in Azerbaijan can only participate in the BICEX auctions indirectly whereas the new off-auction trading will be open to all the seven foreign banks that have received an Azeri banking licence, Sharifov said.
The average turnover in foreign exchange on BICEX is around $3 million a day, according to Farkhad Amirbekov, the general manager of the Baku exchange.
The manat stood at 3.968 to the dollar on Wednesday.
The National Bank is the supervisory authority of BICEX, but Sharifov said the central bank did not wish to control the new off-auction market.

"Trading will be free," he said. "Our aim is to prevent domination (of the market) by a small group of banks and also to prevent any wrong-doing. We will be monitoring computerised trade, but we do not want to control the market."
The main indirect participants are Azeri export industries such as oil, chemicals and cotton processing.

The currency move is a first step towards full convertibility that bankers said would be much easier to proclaim once Azerbaijan has started pumping its new-found deposits in the Caspian Sea and found the means of delivering the oil to Europe.
President Haydar Aliyev said last week during a visit to Moscow that a key oil transportation deal between oil companies of Russia, Azerbaijan and Chechnya was only days away.

Wrangles between Russia and its independence-minded region of Chechnya have held up the agreement, needed before "early" Azeri oil from a major consortium can pass along a pipeline linking Baku to Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiisk.
